        ↓

Jarvis does not directly modify itself.

It creates alternatives and evaluates them.

============================================================
SELF-EVOLUTION SAFETY
============================================================

Self-evolution remains bounded.

Required controls:

- environment isolation
- resource limits
- change limits
- iteration limits
- promotion gates
- rollback
- lineage
- evidence
- human override where configured

No uncontrolled recursive self-modification.

============================================================
PROJECT-INDEPENDENT ARCHITECTURE
============================================================

Building System core APIs must not contain Jarvis-specific assumptions.

Operate on:

- ProjectTarget

- Candidate

- Artifact
- Deployment
- Evidence
- DevelopmentSession

Jarvis becomes one client of Building System.

============================================================

============================================================

External systems enter through adapters.

- RepositoryAdapter
- BuildAdapter

============================================================
OFFLINE-FIRST
============================================================

Building System remains useful offline.

- repository analysis

32. CONTEXT ECONOMICS FOR DEVELOPMENT
The builder should use:
TASK
 ↓
REPOSITORY RETRIEVAL
 ↓
RELEVANT FILES
 ↓
RELEVANT SYMBOLS
 ↓
RELEVANT MEMORY
 ↓
CURRENT ENVIRONMENT STATE
 ↓
CONCISE CONTEXT

Never continuously send:

the complete repository
entire memory
all environment state
full historical logs

to the model.

33. DEVELOPMENT KERNEL
The Building System needs a persistent Development Kernel.
It maintains:

development objective
repository target
environment
active plan
active workers
pending operations
important decisions
blockers
evidence
candidate state
prior attempts
lessons

Kernel state remains outside active model context.
The model receives only a bounded projection.

34. DEVELOPMENT SESSION
A DevelopmentSession represents one complete development objective.
It contains:

session ID
objective
project
workspace
environment
plan
workers
changes
builds
failures
repairs
benchmarks
candidate
promotion state
lessons

The session must be recoverable after interruption where practical.

35. DEVELOPMENT LINEAGE
Jarvis must eventually know:

why code changed
which task caused it
which research finding caused it
which algorithm was selected
which candidate produced it
which benchmark approved it
which promotion created the live version

This lineage becomes essential for future self-evolution.

36. CHANGE INTELLIGENCE
Every meaningful modification must have provenance.
At minimum:

changeId
environmentId
workspaceId
taskId
file
symbol where known
operation
reason
parent change
resulting state

This should let Jarvis answer:
"What changed?"
"Why did it change?"
"What caused it?"
"What depends on it?"
"What happened afterward?"

37. CHANGE SETS
Related modifications should be grouped into a ChangeSet.
A ChangeSet contains:

changeSetId
objective
files
operations
environment
parent version
authoring worker
evidence
status

ChangeSet becomes a unit for:

review
benchmark
promotion
rollback


38. CANDIDATE SYSTEM
Every meaningful experimental result becomes a Candidate.
Candidate
│
├── Candidate ID
├── Parent
├── Lineage
├── Source Snapshot
├── Changes
├── Environment
├── Artifacts
├── Evidence
├── Benchmarks
├── Failures
├── Resource Cost
├── Compatibility
├── Confidence
└── Promotion Status

Possible states:
PROPOSED
→ BUILDING
→ RUNNING
→ EVALUATED
→ PROMOTABLE
→ PROMOTED

or:
REJECTED
FAILED
ABANDONED


39. CANDIDATE GENEALOGY
Example:
CURRENT
 ├── Candidate-A
 │    ├── Candidate-A1
 │    └── Candidate-A2
 │
 └── Candidate-B
      └── Candidate-B1

Jarvis must determine:

parent
descendants
modifications
benchmark differences
why a candidate was selected
why a candidate was rejected


40. EXPERIMENT SPECIFICATION
Create a declarative ExperimentSpecification defining:

objective
target
base state
candidate changes
environment requirements
resource limits
workload
success criteria
benchmark criteria
timeout
iteration limits
retention policy

The experiment must be describable independently of active model context.

41. OPERATION JOURNAL
Create persistent operation history.
Record major operations such as:

environment creation
mutation
file modification
command execution
build
repair
benchmark
deployment
promotion
rollback
destruction

Do not store huge raw logs forever.
Store structured metadata plus retained evidence references.

42. EVIDENCE MODEL
Evidence may represent:

command output
compiler error
runtime observation
benchmark result
resource measurement
deployment health
model output
research finding
comparison result

Important development decisions must be traceable to evidence.

43. OBSERVATION MODEL
Observations are structured, not only raw logs.
Observation may contain:

timestamp
source
environment
process
metric
value
severity
context
evidence reference

Observation may feed:

diagnosis
benchmarking
memory
self-diagnostics
future improvement


44. OPERATION CORRELATION
Important activity must be connectable:
SESSION
→ TASK
→ OPERATION
→ ENVIRONMENT
→ WORKSPACE
→ CHANGE
→ COMMAND
→ BUILD
→ EVIDENCE
→ CANDIDATE
→ PROMOTION

The model should not have to reconstruct this from prose.

45. DEVELOPMENT WORKERS
Workers are bounded temporary execution units.
Possible roles:

Research Worker
Repository Worker
Implementation Worker
Review Worker
Benchmark Worker
Diagnosis Worker
Deployment Worker
Observation Worker

Workers are not permanent personalities.
The central Jarvis remains the orchestrator.

46. WORKER CONTRACT
Every worker receives:

task ID
objective
inputs
allowed capabilities
environment/workspace
resource budget
deadline
expected output

Every worker returns:

status
result
evidence
changes
blockers
confidence
recommended next action

Workers do not automatically create more uncontrolled workers.

47. WORKER MEMORY
Workers must not receive:

complete repository
complete memory
complete world model
complete task history

Each receives only what it needs.
This is central to RAM and context efficiency.

48. WORKER ORCHESTRATION
The Development Orchestrator owns:

worker creation
task assignment
context allocation
resource allocation
cancellation
result collection
conflict handling
worker termination


49. PARALLELIZATION
When the existing PlanGraph determines tasks are independent:
A ─────→ result
B ─────→ result
C ─────→ result

they may run concurrently.
When dependencies exist:
A → B → C

they remain sequential.
Reuse existing planning/dependency architecture.

50. WORKER CONFLICT
If workers disagree:

identify conflict
preserve both results
compare evidence
request additional analysis if necessary
select or synthesize
record the decision

Worker disagreement is evidence, not chaos.

51. RESEARCH WORKER
Produces structured research:

question
sources
findings
mechanisms
limitations
alternatives
confidence
recommendation

Research Worker should not directly modify Jarvis.

52. REPOSITORY WORKER
Answers:

where is X implemented?
what depends on X?
what files matter?
what architecture is involved?
what could this change affect?

Prefer Graphify/repository intelligence over repeated full scans.

53. IMPLEMENTATION WORKER
Implementation Worker may modify only its assigned environment/workspace.
Returns:

changes
files affected
build status
blockers
evidence

It cannot promote its own work.

54. REVIEW WORKER
Review Worker evaluates:

requested behavior
architecture
compatibility
unintended changes
resource impact
candidate quality

Output becomes candidate evidence.

55. BENCHMARK WORKER
Benchmark Worker runs the defined workload against candidates using identical measurement rules.
It must not alter candidate implementation merely to improve scores.

56. DEPLOYMENT WORKER
Deployment Worker handles deployment mechanics.
It does not decide whether promotion should happen.
Promotion remains a separate policy decision.

57. WORKER CANCELLATION
Workers must be cancellable.
Cancellation must:

stop execution
release resources
preserve useful evidence
update task state
avoid orphan processes


58. DEADLINE / BUDGET CONTROL
Every DevelopmentSession may have:

time budget
compute budget
memory budget
worker budget
mutation budget
repair iteration budget

When budget is exhausted:
report:

Insufficient budget to complete.

Do not enter endless loops.

59. IDEMPOTENCY
Retryable operations should be idempotent where practical.
Examples:

environment initialization
dependency installation
artifact registration
state transitions
deployment preparation

Repeated execution must not corrupt development state.

60. CONCURRENCY CONTROL
Prevent multiple workers from silently changing the same workspace.
Use:

ownership
locks
change sets
branch/candidate isolation
merge/reconciliation

Prefer independent candidate environments for competing implementations.

61. MERGE / SYNTHESIS
If candidate A and candidate B contain useful mechanisms:
Candidate A
+
Candidate B
→
Candidate C

Candidate C must be created in a new mutated environment.
Never merge experiments directly into LIVE.

62. ALGORITHM LAB
Provide an abstraction for algorithm experiments.
An AlgorithmExperiment should define:

algorithm identity
implementation
input workload
expected behavior
metrics
baseline
candidate
results

This becomes the foundation for future Algorithm Discovery.

63. BASELINE SYSTEM
Every benchmarkable candidate needs a baseline where appropriate.
BASELINE
vs
CANDIDATE

Use the same workload and resource conditions.
Baseline must be preserved for future regression detection.

64. REGRESSION PROTECTION
Evaluate more than the requested feature.
Track:

baseline behavior
candidate behavior
regression signals

A faster candidate that damages important behavior is not automatically an improvement.

65. PROMOTION DECISION
Promotion combines evidence.
Consider:

correctness
required behavior
benchmark improvement
resource cost
reliability
compatibility
regression risk
confidence
reversibility

Possible outcomes:
PROMOTE
REJECT
NEEDS_MORE_EVIDENCE


66. PROMOTION RECORD
Every promotion creates:

candidate
previous live version
new live version
evidence
decision
reason
timestamp
promotion policy
rollback target

This becomes part of future self-understanding.

67. DEPLOYMENT
Deployment flow:
artifact
→ package
→ stage
→ deploy
→ observe
→ confirm

Deployment is separate from promotion.
Do not allow deployment to silently promote a candidate.

68. DEPLOYMENT ESCALATION
Explicit lifecycle:
EXPERIMENT
→ CANDIDATE
→ STAGED
→ LIVE

Promotion is deliberate.

69. ROLLBACK
Rollback:
LIVE
→ PREVIOUS LIVE

must preserve evidence.
Do not erase failed deployment history.

70. DEPLOYMENT OBSERVATION
After deployment:
deploy
→ observe
→ compare against expected behavior

If health deteriorates:
observe
→ diagnose
→ decide
→ rollback or repair

Do not mutate LIVE automatically without explicit policy.

71. ARTIFACT MANAGEMENT
Artifacts may include:

binaries
APKs
libraries
model artifacts
configurations
packages
data

Artifacts have:

artifactId
environmentId
source commit/version
build identity
dependencies
checksum where applicable
creation metadata

Possible lifecycle:
CREATED
→ VERIFIED
→ CANDIDATE
→ STAGED
→ LIVE
→ ARCHIVED
→ DEPRECATED

Artifact lifetime must remain independent from environment lifetime.

72. ENVIRONMENT RETENTION
Support policies such as:

DESTROY_RUNTIME_KEEP_EVIDENCE
KEEP_ENVIRONMENT
KEEP_ARTIFACTS_ONLY
KEEP_FULL_SNAPSHOT
DESTROY_ALL_NONESSENTIAL_STATE

The default should avoid wasting storage.

73. ENVIRONMENT ADAPTER
Create an EnvironmentAdapter concept supporting:

create
prepare
snapshot
fork
start
stop
inspect
destroy

The first implementation should use the safest practical mechanism available to the repository.
Do not force a specific technology unless required.
The adapter must remain replaceable.

74. RUNTIME ADAPTER
RuntimeAdapter supports:

process lifecycle
service lifecycle
health
logs
resource state
crash detection

Possible runtimes:

local process
container
service
Android
remote runtime

Do not assume only one runtime.

75. REPOSITORY ADAPTER
RepositoryAdapter supports:

inspect
status
branch/snapshot
diff
history
relevant-file retrieval
change application

Git may be the first implementation.
Do not leak Git semantics into every domain model.

76. BUILD ADAPTER
BuildAdapter should expose a normalized interface for:

detect
prepare
build
clean
package
artifact discovery
diagnostics

Support multiple project types.

77. DEPLOYMENT ADAPTER
DeploymentAdapter supports:

prepare
deploy
start
stop
status
health
rollback

It does not decide promotion.

78. MODEL ADAPTER
ModelAdapter supports:

discover
load
invoke
stream where available
cancel
unload
health
resource estimate

The Building System may select different models for different tasks.

79. BENCHMARK ADAPTER
BenchmarkAdapter supports:

workload preparation
execution
measurement
metric collection
normalization
baseline comparison

The benchmark mechanism must remain independent of the candidate implementation.

80. RESEARCH ADAPTER
ResearchAdapter connects the Building System to Universal Research.
Supports:

question
research
extraction
comparison
structured findings

Do not duplicate Universal Research.

81. CANDIDATE EVALUATION
Evaluation should consider:

correctness
functional requirements
latency
resource efficiency
reliability
compatibility
regression risk
evidence quality
confidence
reversibility

Evaluation should output:

PROMOTE
REJECT
NEEDS_MORE_EVIDENCE


82. REPRODUCIBILITY
Every experiment should record:

source version
environment specification
dependency versions
configuration
model used
worker configuration
algorithm candidate
workload
resource policy

Jarvis should be able to reconstruct a previous experiment.

83. OPERATION RECOVERY
If Jarvis stops during development:
On restart:

discover persistent sessions
identify incomplete operations
inspect environments
inspect processes
reconcile state
mark uncertain operations
resume, retry, rollback, or destroy safely

Never infer success from incomplete state.

84. ORPHAN CLEANUP
Detect and clean:

orphan processes
orphan workers
orphan environments
temporary files
stale locks
expired artifacts
abandoned sessions

Preserve evidence needed for learning before destruction.

85. STATE RECONCILIATION
Recorded state and real state may diverge.
Examples:
RECORDED: RUNNING
ACTUAL: process dead

RECORDED: DESTROYED
ACTUAL: environment exists

RECORDED: BUILDING
ACTUAL: build process gone

Detect and safely reconcile.

86. DEVELOPMENT MEMORY
Use existing Jarvis memory.
Development events should become structured experiences such as:

objective
repository state
selected approach
research findings
implementation decisions
failed approaches
successful repairs
benchmark outcomes
deployment outcomes
rollback events
lessons

Do not permanently store every command output.
Store future-value information.

87. DEVELOPMENT KNOWLEDGE GRAPH
Integrate development knowledge into the existing Galaxy/Knowledge Graph.
Represent:
PROJECT
→ contains
COMPONENT

COMPONENT
→ depends_on
COMPONENT

TASK
→ modified
COMPONENT

RESEARCH
→ influenced
DECISION

DECISION
→ produced
CANDIDATE

CANDIDATE
→ tested_in
ENVIRONMENT

CANDIDATE
→ produced
ARTIFACT

BENCHMARK
→ evaluated
CANDIDATE

PROMOTION
→ promoted
CANDIDATE

ROLLBACK
→ reverted
PROMOTION

Do not create another graph system.

88. LESSON EXTRACTION
After completed development:
experience
→ extract lesson
→ determine reuse potential
→ store

Examples:

build system required X
failure pattern Y usually means Z
algorithm A outperforms B under memory pressure
library X conflicts with Y
repair strategy Z succeeded under condition Q

These lessons become reusable engineering knowledge.

89. DESIGN MEMORY
Important architecture decisions should become durable memory.
Record:
DECISION
→ ALTERNATIVES
→ SELECTED MECHANISM
→ REASON
→ EVIDENCE
→ CONSEQUENCES

This prevents Jarvis from rediscovering the same architecture repeatedly.

90. OPERATIONAL MEMORY
The Building System should remember not only facts, but useful engineering behavior.
Example:
Problem
→ attempted solution
→ result
→ successful solution
→ context in which it worked

This is separate from raw logs.
It is reusable operational knowledge.

91. LEARNING
Learning should occur at multiple levels:
EXPERIENCE
│
├── FACT LEARNING
├── PROCEDURAL LEARNING
├── USER LEARNING
├── FAILURE LEARNING
├── STRATEGY LEARNING
├── TOOL LEARNING
├── ARCHITECTURE LEARNING
└── MODEL / ALGORITHM LEARNING

The system should preserve useful engineering rules.
Do not require weight changes for every form of learning.

92. PERSISTENT BEHAVIORAL RULES
When repeated experience establishes a useful rule:
experience
→ evidence
→ recurring pattern
→ validated rule
→ persistent behavioral knowledge

Rules must be:

evidence-backed
scoped
revisable
attributable to source experience

Do not turn every single event into permanent behavior.

93. RESEARCH MEMORY
Research should remain traceable:
RESEARCH QUESTION
→ SOURCE
→ MECHANISM
→ DECISION
→ IMPLEMENTATION
→ RESULT

This creates a chain from knowledge discovery to engineering outcome.

94. SELF-DEVELOPMENT FOUNDATION
The Building System must eventually be able to target:
ANY SOFTWARE PROJECT

and:
JARVIS ITSELF

Use ProjectTarget rather than hardcoding Jarvis.
Possible targets:

Jarvis
external repository
workspace
application
service
algorithm
capability


95. JARVIS SELF-DEVELOPMENT LOOP
Once the generic Building System exists:
JARVIS
→ identifies limitation
→ researches solution
→ extracts mechanism
→ designs candidate
→ snapshots current system
→ creates mutated Jarvis environment
→ implements change
→ builds
→ executes
→ observes
→ benchmarks
→ compares against current
→ stages
→ promotion decision

Live Jarvis remains protected during experimentation.

96. SELF-EVOLUTION SAFETY
Self-evolution remains bounded.
Controls include:

environment isolation
resource limits
change limits
iteration limits
promotion gates
rollback
lineage
evidence
human override where configured

Never create unrestricted recursive self-modification.

97. SELF-REPLACEMENT
Individual organs may eventually be treated as candidate implementations.
Example:
CURRENT MEMORY RETRIEVAL
        ↓
CANDIDATE A
CANDIDATE B
CANDIDATE C
        ↓
SAME WORKLOAD
        ↓
BENCHMARK
        ↓
COMPARE
        ↓
PROMOTION

This permits evolution of individual mechanisms without replacing the entire organism.

98. WHOLE-SYSTEM EVOLUTION
Eventually:
Jarvis
→ identifies opportunity
→ creates architecture candidate
→ forks system
→ mutates multiple organs
→ builds candidate
→ runs workloads
→ observes behavior
→ compares baseline
→ selects candidate
→ stages
→ promotes

Do not activate unrestricted whole-system evolution during the current build.
Build the machinery that makes bounded evolution possible.

99. BUILDING SYSTEM AS AN ORGAN
The Building System should eventually be a true Jarvis organ.
Relationship:
COGNITION
→ decides what should exist

RESEARCH
→ discovers how it could exist

BUILDING SYSTEM
→ constructs it

MUTATED ENVIRONMENT
→ provides alternative reality

CAPABILITY FABRIC
→ provides actions

OBSERVATION
→ determines what happened

MEMORY
→ preserves what was learned

KNOWLEDGE GRAPH
→ preserves relationships

SELF MODEL
→ understands what changed

NERVOUS SYSTEM
→ coordinates the organism

This is how Jarvis can eventually create new organs.

100. FUTURE ORGAN CREATION
The architecture must eventually support creation of:

new capability
new algorithm
new memory mechanism
new research mechanism
new perception organ
new voice capability
new vision capability
new UI
new application
new service
new model adapter
new environment type
new development strategy

without requiring the Building System itself to be fundamentally rewritten for each category.

101. BUILDING SYSTEM SELF-EXTENSION
If Jarvis discovers:

"The Building System itself is inefficient."

it should eventually be able to use the same mechanism:
CURRENT BUILDING SYSTEM
→ SNAPSHOT
→ CANDIDATE
→ MUTATED ENVIRONMENT
→ IMPROVEMENT
→ BENCHMARK
→ COMPARE
→ PROMOTE

The Building System is not exempt from evolution.
It is protected by the same promotion boundary.

102. EVENT MODEL
The Building System must integrate with the existing event/nervous-system architecture.
Meaningful events include, where applicable:

development session requested
session state changed
environment requested
environment created
environment prepared
environment started
environment stopped
environment mutated
environment destroyed
workspace created
workspace changed
repository analyzed
research requested
research completed
mechanism extracted
candidate created
candidate mutated
change created
change applied
command started
command completed
build started
build completed
build failed
process started
process stopped
observation created
diagnosis created
repair attempted
repair succeeded
repair failed
benchmark started
benchmark completed
candidate evaluated
candidate rejected
candidate marked promotable
staging started
deployment started
deployment completed
promotion requested
promotion approved
promotion rejected
rollback requested
rollback completed
artifact created
lesson extracted
worker created
worker completed
worker cancelled
budget exhausted
recovery started
recovery completed

Do not create a second event bus.

103. OBSERVABILITY
The Building System must expose structured information about:

current development session
current phase
active environments
active workers
active builds
running processes
resource consumption
candidate status
benchmark status
deployment status
failures
recovery

The system should be understandable to:

Jarvis
future UI
human operator
future Stage 16 diagnostic system

Avoid enormous continuous logs when structured state is sufficient.

104. LOCAL HEALTH
Health information should exist for:

environments
workspaces
builds
processes
artifacts
deployments

Use existing health infrastructure where possible.
Do not build the final system-wide diagnostic fabric here.

105. DEVELOPMENT CONTROL INTERFACE
The Building System should provide a local operational interface, programmatic and/or CLI-based, for:

sessions
environments
workspaces
experiments
candidates
benchmarks
deployments
promotions
rollbacks
recovery
cleanup

Underlying domain services must be shared.
Do not create a second logic path for the CLI.

106. DEVELOPMENT DASHBOARD CONTRACT
Expose enough structured state that a future UI can visualize:

sessions
environment genealogy
candidate genealogy
active workers
builds
benchmarks
deployment status
failures
resources
promotion state
rollback history

Polished UI is not the main purpose of the current build.
Build the underlying organism.

107. SECURITY / TRUST BOUNDARY
The environment boundary is a trust boundary.
The system must distinguish:
EXPERIMENTAL
STAGED
LIVE

Architecture must enforce this distinction.
Do not rely only on the model remembering not to modify LIVE.

108. PERMISSIONS
Development capabilities must have explicit permission classes.
Examples:

READ_WORKSPACE
WRITE_WORKSPACE
EXECUTE_PROCESS
INSTALL_DEPENDENCY
CREATE_ENVIRONMENT
DEPLOY
PROMOTE
ROLLBACK

Experimental permission may be broader than LIVE permission.
Promotion must be separately controlled.

109. SECRET ISOLATION
Do not unnecessarily expose:

API keys
authentication tokens
passwords
private credentials
live service secrets

inside experimental environments.
Do not persist secrets inside:

experiment evidence
memory
source snapshots
candidate metadata
operation logs


110. NETWORK POLICY
Experimental network access should be policy-controlled.
Possible conceptual modes:
OFFLINE
RESTRICTED
ALLOWED

Default to minimal access needed for the task.
Record whether experimental success depended on network access.

111. EXPERIMENT CONTAMINATION CONTROL
An experiment should not silently depend upon undeclared:

host files
environment variables
services
network resources
credentials

Relevant external dependencies should be recorded.
This improves reproducibility.

112. OFFLINE-FIRST
The Building System should remain useful offline.
It should be capable of:

repository analysis
code modification
local builds
local execution
local experiments
local benchmarks
local deployment
local memory
local model use

without requiring cloud services.
Cloud may be an optional accelerator later.

113. CLOUD CODE BOUNDARY
Cloud Code is an external development accelerator.
It may be used now to build Jarvis.
It must never become a Jarvis runtime dependency.
Later, Cloud Code may become:

external research source
optional worker
optional development capability

but never the foundation of Jarvis's existence.

114. OMNIROUTE BOUNDARY
OmniRoute may accelerate model routing during development.
It must not become a hardcoded Jarvis runtime dependency.
Jarvis should communicate with models through the existing ModelManager / ModelProvider abstractions.
The local model architecture must remain capable of operating without OmniRoute.

115. GRAPHIFY BOUNDARY
Graphify may accelerate repository intelligence.
It must not become the only repository understanding mechanism.
The Building System needs an abstraction that can query or replace Graphify.
If Graphify is unavailable, Jarvis must retain a fallback repository inspection path.

116. EXTERNAL RESEARCH BOUNDARY
Mem0, Prime-Agent, Multi-Agent systems research, LFM, Graphify, OpenAlternative, and other external sources are research inputs.
They are not automatically Jarvis architecture.
The process remains:
DISCOVER
→ RESEARCH
→ UNDERSTAND MECHANISM
→ IDENTIFY STRENGTHS
→ IDENTIFY LIMITATIONS
→ FIND ALTERNATIVES
→ GENERALIZE
→ SYNTHESIZE
→ JARVIS-NATIVE IMPLEMENTATION


117. BUILDING SYSTEM RESEARCH SYNTHESIS
The Building System should explicitly absorb useful mechanisms from:
Mem0
Relevant mechanism classes:

extraction
consolidation
selective retrieval
memory history
relationship-aware memory
evidence-backed memory

Do not build Mem0 inside Jarvis.
Use the existing memory architecture.
Prime-Agent
Relevant mechanism classes:

externalized state
kernel outside context
bounded workers
delegation
task lineage
iterative repair
learning from outcomes

Do not reproduce the exact Prime-Agent architecture.
Multi-Agent Systems Research
Relevant mechanism classes:

role specialization
orchestration
structured worker communication
bounded worker context
parallelization
evaluation
shared objective

Do not build a permanent uncontrolled swarm.
LFM
Relevant mechanism classes:

efficient local inference
adaptive computation
model specialization
low-memory execution
retrieval specialization
edge deployment
task-specific intelligence

Do not make a vendor dependency.

118. RESEARCH → BUILDING PIPELINE
The complete research-to-building pipeline is:
PROBLEM
 ↓
UNDERSTAND
 ↓
RESEARCH
 ↓
SOURCE COLLECTION
 ↓
MECHANISM EXTRACTION
 ↓
STRENGTHS
 ↓
LIMITATIONS
 ↓
ALTERNATIVES
 ↓
GENERALIZATION
 ↓
DESIGN
 ↓
CANDIDATE
 ↓
MUTATED ENVIRONMENT
 ↓
IMPLEMENT
 ↓
RUN
 ↓
BENCHMARK
 ↓
COMPARE
 ↓
PROMOTE / REJECT


119. ALGORITHM DISCOVERY
Future Algorithm Discovery should use:
PROBLEM
 ↓
KNOWN ALGORITHMS
 ↓
RESEARCH
 ↓
GENERATE VARIANTS
 ↓
MUTATED ENVIRONMENTS
 ↓
BENCHMARK
 ↓
COMPARE
 ↓
SELECT

Algorithms may target:

retrieval
ranking
planning
scheduling
routing
memory
compression
orchestration

model selection

The Building System becomes the execution substrate for Algorithm Discovery.

120. MODEL EVOLUTION RESEARCH
Future model evolution may use:
MODEL PROBLEM
 ↓
RESEARCH
 ↓
ARCHITECTURE ANALYSIS
 ↓
COMPUTATIONAL BOTTLENECK
 ↓
HYPOTHESIS
 ↓
EXPERIMENT
 ↓
MODEL VARIANT
 ↓
TRAIN / FINE-TUNE / DISTILL / ADAPT
 ↓
BENCHMARK
 ↓
COMPARE

This is where the concept of Jarvis learning from efficient architectures such as LFM becomes useful.
The system should research the mechanism rather than blindly imitate a vendor.

121. SELF-MODIFICATION CONCEPT
Self-modification does not mean:

Jarvis randomly edits its own model weights or source code.

The preferred long-term architecture is:
EXPERIENCE
 ↓
OBSERVATION
 ↓
PATTERN
 ↓
HYPOTHESIS
 ↓
RESEARCH
 ↓
EXPERIMENT
 ↓
CANDIDATE
 ↓
BENCHMARK
 ↓
EVIDENCE
 ↓
PROMOTION

Potential targets include:

prompting
routing
memory policy
retrieval
algorithms
tools
workflows
code
models
quantization
runtime
specialization
adapters
fine-tuning

ChatGPT:
Yes. This is actually useful for Jarvis — but mainly as an algorithm/inference-mechanism research source, not as something we should install as Jarvis's brain.
The repo is unusually relevant to the problem you've been trying to solve: how to get extremely large model capacity onto limited RAM by changing where computation and model state live.
What is genuinely valuable
The project implements Kimi K3 inference in portable C99, with no BLAS, framework, or GPU, and reports 8.24 GB peak RSS for a 2.78T-parameter model. The trick is not that 2.78T parameters somehow fit in RAM; most of the checkpoint stays on disk and is streamed as needed. 
The most interesting mechanisms are:
1. On-demand expert streaming
K3 is MoE: only 16 of 896 routed experts are activated per token. The implementation keeps those experts off-RAM and reads the required ones from NVMe, even multiplying directly from packed 4-bit weights rather than fully dequantizing them. 
That is highly relevant to your RAM-conservation architecture.
Instead of:
Load entire model
→ RAM
→ infer

you get:
Task
 ↓
router
 ↓
needed experts
 ↓
load only what is needed
 ↓
compute
 ↓
release/cache

2. Memory-budgeted model residency
The repo explicitly exposes different memory presets and shows that increasing RAM mainly changes speed, while the generated output remains byte-identical in its reported runs. It also splits the model into a resident "trunk" and streamed routed experts. 
That maps beautifully onto the Jarvis principle:

RAM should be a budget, not a prerequisite for intelligence.

This could inspire a general Model Residency Governor inside Jarvis.
3. Incremental decoding / state reuse
The --incremental path carries the KV cache and recurrent state between tokens instead of recomputing the entire prefix. The repo explicitly notes that without this, each step re-runs the prefix at O(T²); incremental generation makes later token steps fixed-cost relative to the prefix. 
This is exactly the kind of mechanism that belongs in Jarvis's future inference efficiency layer.
4. KDA / recurrent state
The repo's implementation is built around Kimi K3's KDA architecture and carries recurrent KDA state along with the KV cache. The broader K3 architecture uses 69 KDA attention layers and 24 gated MLA layers, plus Attention Residuals and Stable LatentMoE. 
We should study the mechanism, not copy the entire architecture.
5. Exact computation with a tiny engine
The engine itself is only about 176 KB according to the repo's measurements, because the giant model weights are not treated as application-resident RAM. 
That is conceptually important for your offline Jarvis:

runtime intelligence infrastructure can be tiny while the model substrate is huge and selectively materialized.


There's also a very interesting algorithmic toolbox in the repo
The README explicitly exposes:

checkpoint header parsing
strict configuration parsing
byte-accurate tokenizer
packed expert loading
memory-budgeted trunk/expert placement
incremental decoding
KV cache + recurrent state reuse
expert cache tracing
capacity simulation
logit comparison
deterministic output checking
partial-layer execution
configurable memory presets

The expert-cache trace + simulator is especially interesting for your future Builder/Research system because Jarvis could eventually use the same pattern:
RUN
 ↓
capture access pattern
 ↓
simulate different memory budgets
 ↓
estimate cache behavior
 ↓
choose residency policy
 ↓
benchmark

That's not just an inference trick — it's a general resource-optimization methodology.

But there is a huge catch
Do not try to run Kimi K3 on your phone.
The repository reports the 8 GB configuration at roughly 26.5 seconds/token, with 128 GB around 5.6 seconds/token, and the K3 checkpoint is roughly 1.56 TB on disk. 
So this is not your local Jarvis model solution.
It is a research source for the architecture of efficient inference.
And there's an even more important insight:
K3 itself uses architectural tricks such as KDA, MLA, Attention Residuals, and sparse MoE routing; this C implementation adds a second layer of system-level optimization by deciding what stays resident and what gets streamed. 
That's exactly the distinction we want in Jarvis:
MODEL ARCHITECTURE
        +
INFERENCE RUNTIME ARCHITECTURE
        +
RESOURCE / RESIDENCY ARCHITECTURE
        +
TASK ROUTING

Not just "find a smaller model."

What I would extract for Jarvis
I would add this repository to the LFM research family, but as a separate mechanism branch:
EFFICIENT INTELLIGENCE RESEARCH
│
├── LFM
│   ├── adaptive compute
│   ├── specialization
│   └── efficient architectures
│
└── Kimi K3-in-C
    ├── sparse expert activation
    ├── on-demand expert streaming
    ├── memory-budgeted residency
    ├── packed-weight computation
    ├── incremental decoding
    ├── recurrent-state reuse
    ├── cache simulation
    ├── workload tracing
    └── deterministic capacity/performance comparison

Then Jarvis can generalize the mechanism:

Keep only the computational state that is valuable right now resident; retrieve/materialize the rest on demand.

That could eventually apply not only to models, but to:

memory
tools
workers
environments
code indexes
research corpora
algorithms
capabilities

So yes — save this one. It has real research value for your Jarvis architecture.
I would not install it into Jarvis yet. I would put it into the vault as a research seed / mechanism source, then let the future Universal Research + Building System decide which parts are worth implementing natively.

2. Claude Squad — very high value
This one directly addresses your complaint that Claude Code works too slowly.
It manages multiple Claude Code instances in isolated Git workspaces, allowing concurrent tasks and background execution. It uses tmux plus Git worktrees, and its default program is Claude Code.

rather than one turtle doing everything sequentially.

# JARVIS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY

## 1. PROJECT AUTHORITY

The Jarvis vault roadmap and architecture documents are authoritative.

Before major implementation work, read the relevant vault specification.

Do not replace Jarvis architecture with generic agent architecture.

## 2. TOOL ROLE SEPARATION

Superpowers:
Development methodology, planning, debugging, review, bounded subagent workflows.

BMAD:
Large-project requirements, architecture, and delivery planning.

Karpathy:
Behavioral discipline: verify assumptions, avoid overengineering, make surgical changes, surface uncertainty.

Anthropic Skills:
Specialized capabilities such as documents and frontend design.

Context7:
Current external library/API documentation.

Graphify:
Repository structure, symbol/dependency relationships, targeted codebase retrieval.

Claude Squad:
Parallel Claude Code sessions/worktrees.

Ralph:
Bounded repeated implementation loops using fresh contexts.

Playwright:
Browser execution and UI observation.

Archon:
Higher-level workflow/session orchestration when explicitly requested.

SuperClaude:
Optional command/mode/toolbox layer; it does not override Jarvis architecture.

Slavingia:
Business/product skills only when relevant to business work.

OmniRoute:
External model routing only; not Jarvis architecture.

## 3. JARVIS RULES OVERRIDE GENERIC TOOL DEFAULTS

This repository deliberately does NOT use a separate giant testing phase.

Do not launch a 500+ test-generation effort for ordinary builds.

Verification is proportional to the build and must not replace implementation.

The vault roadmap is the authority.

## 4. MODEL CONTEXT ECONOMY

Do not read the entire repository unless explicitly required.

Use Graphify/repository retrieval for structure.

Use Context7 for external documentation.

Use bounded context.

Keep durable state in files/memory rather than repeatedly filling model context.

## 5. PARALLEL WORK

Parallelize only independent tasks.

Use Claude Squad/worktrees for parallel implementation.

Do not let multiple workers edit the same worktree simultaneously.

## 6. LONG RUNNING WORK

Use Ralph only for explicitly bounded PRDs/stories.

Never use Ralph to autonomously reinterpret the entire Jarvis roadmap.

## 7. EXTERNAL TOOLS

External projects are mechanisms or tools, not automatic Jarvis architecture.

Extract useful mechanisms and integrate them Jarvis-natively.

## 8. STOP CONDITIONS

Do not continue into unrelated roadmap stages.

Do not silently redesign the architecture.

Do not install additional frameworks simply because they appear useful.

Ask for no clarification when the vault roadmap already determines the answer.

This is the governor that makes the tools cooperate.

==================================================
THIRD: ESTABLISH TOOL RESPONSIBILITY
==================================================

Create a clear hierarchy so the tools do not fight each other.

Authority order:

1. Jarvis vault roadmap/specification
2. Jarvis CLAUDE.md/project rules
3. Claude Code core behavior
4. specialized skills and methods
5. external orchestration tools

Roles:

Superpowers
→ engineering methodology, planning, debugging, review, bounded subagent workflows

Karpathy Skills
→ discipline, assumption checking, simplicity, surgical changes, goal-driven execution

BMAD
→ large-project requirements, architecture, planning, delivery workflows

SuperClaude
→ optional commands, modes, specialized command patterns, and supporting integrations

Anthropic Skills
→ official specialized skills

Anthropic frontend-design
→ UI/frontend design tasks only

Context7
→ current external library/API documentation

Graphify
→ repository structure, symbols, dependencies, targeted codebase retrieval

Claude Squad
→ parallel Claude Code sessions and isolated worktrees

Ralph
→ bounded long-running iterative implementation loops

Playwright
→ browser automation and UI observation

Archon
→ optional higher-level workflow/session orchestration

Slavingia Skills
→ business/product work only

OmniRoute
→ model routing/provider transport only

NO TOOL MAY OVERRIDE THE JARVIS ARCHITECTURE.

==================================================
FOURTH: CONFIGURE AUTOMATIC TOOL SELECTION
==================================================

The point is:

I should NOT have to say:

"use Graphify"

"use Context7"

"use Playwright"

"use Superpowers"

"use BMAD"

etc.

Claude must automatically select the appropriate tool based on the task.

Examples:

Repository question
→ Graphify

External library/API question
→ Context7

Planning a large subsystem
→ BMAD/Superpowers as appropriate

Implementation
→ Claude Code + Superpowers methodology

Parallel independent work
→ Claude Squad

Bounded repeated implementation loop
→ Ralph

Browser/UI interaction
→ Playwright

Official document skill
→ Anthropic Skills

Frontend design
→ frontend-design skill

Business/product work
→ Slavingia Skills

Workflow/session orchestration when beneficial
→ Archon

Model provider routing
→ OmniRoute

Do not invoke all tools for every task.

Use the minimum sufficient toolset.

==================================================
FIFTH: CONFIGURE OMNIROUTE
==================================================

OmniRoute is already installed.

Inspect its configuration and existing profile.

Do not ask me for the API key if it is already stored in OmniRoute.

Do not create duplicate provider profiles.

Determine:

- server status
- configured profiles
- API endpoint
- configured model routes
- Claude Code integration
- available provider connections

Claude Code must be able to use OmniRoute when appropriate.

Do not hardcode OmniRoute as a permanent Jarvis runtime dependency.

It is a development/model-routing layer.

==================================================
SIXTH: CONFIGURE GRAPHIFY
==================================================

Graphify is already installed.

The Jarvis repository contains a large corpus.

Ensure:

- repository graph exists
- the correct repository scope is indexed
- the graph is current
- Claude can retrieve repository intelligence
- the integration is available from the Jarvis project

Do not repeatedly re-index the entire repository unnecessarily.

If Graphify has a Claude Code skill/integration, install or configure it.

If it does not, create the smallest project integration required.

Graphify should remain a repository intelligence layer, not the source of truth.

==================================================
SEVENTH: CONFIGURE CONTEXT7
==================================================

Configure Context7 for Claude Code.

Ensure Claude can retrieve current documentation for external libraries and APIs.

Verify that Context7 is callable from Claude.

Do not create duplicate Context7 integrations.

==================================================
EIGHTH: CONFIGURE ANTHROPIC SKILLS
==================================================

Configure the official Anthropic skills marketplace/repository.

Ensure the useful official skills are available to Claude.

Do not duplicate frontend-design if already provided by the official skill package.

Make frontend-design automatically available for frontend/UI tasks.

==================================================
NINTH: CONFIGURE SUPERPOWERS
==================================================

Install/configure Superpowers correctly for Claude Code if not already active.

Ensure its skills are available.

Do NOT allow it to override Jarvis project rules.

IMPORTANT:
This project deliberately removed the massive dedicated test phase.

Do not let generic workflow guidance turn every Jarvis build into a 500+ test-generation task.

Respect the Jarvis project instructions.

==================================================
TENTH: CONFIGURE KARPATHY SKILLS
==================================================

Configure the Karpathy guidance so Claude follows its useful engineering principles.

Preserve the existing Jarvis CLAUDE.md.

Do not replace it.

Resolve the hierarchy explicitly:

Jarvis architecture/rules
→ remain authoritative

Karpathy principles
→ improve implementation behavior

==================================================
ELEVENTH: CONFIGURE BMAD
==================================================

Configure BMAD for this project.

Ensure its Claude Code support is available.

Do not allow BMAD to replace the Jarvis roadmap.

BMAD is a planning/workflow mechanism.

Jarvis vault specifications remain authoritative.

==================================================
TWELFTH: CONFIGURE SUPERCLAUDE
==================================================

Configure SuperClaude only after inspecting existing Claude integrations.

Avoid duplicate functionality.

Do NOT enable every optional integration automatically.

Only enable mechanisms that improve:

- research
- code navigation
- reasoning
- implementation
- review
- documentation
- task management

Do not create conflicting MCP servers.

==================================================
THIRTEENTH: CONFIGURE CLAUDE SQUAD
==================================================

Configure Claude Squad for parallel development.

Verify:

- tmux
- git
- worktrees
- Claude executable path

Important:

Never allow multiple workers to modify the same mutable worktree simultaneously.

Use separate worktrees/branches for parallel tasks.

Claude Squad should be used automatically when a task is genuinely parallelizable.

Do not spawn parallel workers for trivial sequential work.

==================================================
FOURTEENTH: CONFIGURE RALPH
==================================================

Configure Ralph's Claude Code skills/commands.

Ralph should be used only for bounded long-running implementation loops.

Rules:

- bounded task
- explicit objective
- explicit completion condition
- iteration limit
- no autonomous reinterpretation of Jarvis architecture

Do not use Ralph to independently decide the entire Jarvis roadmap.

==================================================
FIFTEENTH: CONFIGURE PLAYWRIGHT
==================================================

Install/configure Playwright so Claude can use browser automation where required.

Verify browser availability.

If possible, ensure Chromium is installed.

Do NOT make Playwright part of unrelated backend tasks.

Use it automatically for:

- web UI
- browser behavior
- browser-based debugging
- frontend verification
- web application interaction

==================================================
SIXTEENTH: CONFIGURE ARCHON
==================================================

Archon is a higher-level orchestration layer.

Configure it only after lower-level components are working.

Do not allow Archon to compete with:

- BMAD
- Superpowers
- Claude Squad
- Ralph

Instead establish:

Archon
→ workflow/session orchestration when useful

Superpowers
→ execution methodology

BMAD
→ planning methodology

Claude Squad
→ parallel workers

Ralph
→ bounded iterative loop

If Archon duplicates a function already handled better by another installed mechanism, do not activate the duplicate path by default.

==================================================
SEVENTEENTH: CONFIGURE SLAVINGIA SKILLS
==================================================

Configure Slavingia skills if they are not already available.

They should be treated as business/product skills.

Do not activate them during ordinary Jarvis engineering unless the task is actually business/product related.

==================================================
EIGHTEENTH: CREATE THE MASTER TOOL POLICY
==================================================

Create/update:

/sdcard/jarvis-repo/CLAUDE.md

Do not destroy existing project instructions.

Back up the old file first.

The resulting CLAUDE.md must explicitly establish:

ROLE:
You are the primary Jarvis development intelligence.

AUTHORITY:
Vault architecture/roadmaps and project rules override external workflows.

TOOL ROUTING:
Use the appropriate installed capability automatically.

REPOSITORY:
Use Graphify for structural repository understanding.

DOCUMENTATION:
Use Context7 for current external APIs/docs.

ENGINEERING:
Use Superpowers/Karpathy principles.

PLANNING:
Use BMAD when large-scale planning is required.

PARALLELIZATION:
Use Claude Squad for genuinely independent work.

ITERATION:
Use Ralph for bounded long-running tasks.

BROWSER:
Use Playwright when browser interaction is required.

ORCHESTRATION:
Use Archon only when it genuinely improves workflow/session orchestration.

MODEL ROUTING:
Use OmniRoute when configured and appropriate.

FRONTEND:
Use Anthropic frontend-design skill when applicable.

BUSINESS:
Use Slavingia skills only when applicable.

SCOPE:
Do not activate all tools for every task.

==================================================
NINETEENTH: TOOL CONFLICT RULES
==================================================

Resolve conflicts in this order:

PROJECT REQUIREMENTS
→ JARVIS ARCHITECTURE
→ TASK REQUIREMENTS
→ TOOL CAPABILITY
→ TOOL DEFAULT BEHAVIOR

If two tools provide overlapping functionality:

choose one primary owner.

Examples:

Superpowers vs BMAD:
BMAD plans large work.
Superpowers executes engineering methodology.

Superpowers vs Karpathy:
Superpowers provides workflow.
Karpathy provides discipline.
Jarvis rules override both.

Claude Squad vs Ralph:
Squad provides parallel workers.
Ralph provides bounded repeated iteration.
They can be combined when justified.

Archon vs everything:
Archon is optional orchestration, not authority.

Graphify vs Context7:
Graphify = internal repo.
Context7 = external libraries.

OmniRoute:
model routing only.

Do not let overlapping tools independently make contradictory plans for the same task.

Do not silently assume shared storage behaves like ext4.

==================================================

If shared storage causes problems:

determine a safe development workspace strategy.

Do not silently move the Jarvis repository.

Do not create a second copy of the project without recording why.

If an alternate worktree root is required:

document:

source repository
worktree root
synchronization strategy
cleanup policy

temporary

==================================================

3. inspect dependencies

==================================================
NINETIETH: VERIFICATION PHILOSOPHY
==================================================

Verification should be proportional to risk.

Low-risk change:

targeted verification

Medium-risk feature:

build
+
behavior verification
+
relevant regression checks

High-risk subsystem:

architecture review
+
build
+
behavior verification
+
resource analysis
+
failure-path verification
+
relevant regression checks

Do not generate huge test suites simply to satisfy a generic methodology.

Quality is more important than test volume.

==================================================
NINETY-FIRST: TESTING BOUNDARY
==================================================

Testing is one verification mechanism.

It is not the entire verification system.

Use:

static analysis
build results
runtime behavior
targeted tests
integration checks
browser observation
benchmarks
resource measurements
manual inspection

where appropriate.

Choose evidence based on risk.

==================================================
NINETY-SECOND: REGRESSION PROTECTION
==================================================

Before changing important behavior:

identify known behavior that must remain intact.

After changing:

verify the changed behavior
+
verify important unaffected behavior

Do not assume:

"build passed"

means:

"system is correct."

==================================================
NINETY-THIRD: BUILD FAILURE LOOP
==================================================

If a build fails:

BUILD
 ↓
CAPTURE FAILURE
 ↓
CLASSIFY
 ↓
LOCATE CAUSE
 ↓
PATCH
 ↓
BUILD AGAIN

Limit repair iterations.

If repeated repair fails:

stop.

Report:

what failed
what was attempted
what evidence exists
what remains blocked

Do not enter an endless repair loop.

==================================================
NINETY-FOURTH: RUNTIME FAILURE LOOP
==================================================

If runtime behavior fails:

RUN
 ↓
OBSERVE
 ↓
CLASSIFY
 ↓
DIAGNOSE
 ↓
PATCH
 ↓
RUN AGAIN

Preserve the original failure evidence.

Do not overwrite the evidence with only the final successful state.

==================================================
NINETY-FIFTH: WORKER FAILURE
==================================================

If a worker fails:

do not immediately spawn unlimited replacements.

Determine:

failure type
remaining budget
whether the task is still valid
whether another worker is appropriate
whether the main session should take over

Terminate failed workers cleanly.

Preserve useful evidence.

==================================================
NINETY-SIXTH: PARALLELIZATION THRESHOLD
==================================================

Parallelize only when:

tasks are genuinely independent
+
the coordination cost is justified.

Good candidate:

three independent repository investigations.

Poor candidate:

three workers editing the same function.

Poor candidate:

tiny five-minute task.

The goal is increased throughput, not maximum worker count.

==================================================
NINETY-SEVENTH: SYNTHESIS AFTER PARALLEL WORK
==================================================

Parallel worker results must return to a central synthesis point.

The synthesis process:

collect
→ normalize
→ compare
→ detect conflicts
→ inspect evidence
→ select/synthesize
→ implement intentionally

Do not blindly concatenate worker outputs.

==================================================

==================================================

When external research is required:

prefer authoritative sources.

Separate:

FACT
INFERENCE
HYPOTHESIS
RECOMMENDATION

Do not turn an unverified claim into architecture.

For technical libraries:

prefer official documentation and current version information.

Use Context7 where appropriate.

Then determine:

Should Jarvis adapt it?

Should Jarvis redesign it?

Should Jarvis reject it?

==================================================NINETIETH: VERIFICATION PHILOSOPHY
Verification should be proportional to risk.
Low-risk change:
targeted verification
Medium-risk feature:
build+behavior verification+relevant regression checks
High-risk subsystem:
architecture review+build+behavior verification+resource analysis+failure-path verification+relevant regression checks
Do not generate huge test suites simply to satisfy a generic methodology.
Quality is more important than test volume.
==================================================NINETY-FIRST: TESTING BOUNDARY
Testing is one verification mechanism.
It is not the entire verification system.
Use:
static analysisbuild resultsruntime behaviortargeted testsintegration checksbrowser observationbenchmarksresource measurementsmanual inspection
where appropriate.
Choose evidence based on risk.
==================================================NINETY-SECOND: REGRESSION PROTECTION
Before changing important behavior:
identify known behavior that must remain intact.
After changing:
verify the changed behavior+verify important unaffected behavior
Do not assume:
"build passed"
means:
"system is correct."
==================================================NINETY-THIRD: BUILD FAILURE LOOP
If a build fails:
BUILD ↓CAPTURE FAILURE ↓CLASSIFY ↓LOCATE CAUSE ↓PATCH ↓BUILD AGAIN
Limit repair iterations.
If repeated repair fails:
stop.
Report:
what failedwhat was attemptedwhat evidence existswhat remains blocked
Do not enter an endless repair loop.
==================================================NINETY-FOURTH: RUNTIME FAILURE LOOP
If runtime behavior fails:
RUN ↓OBSERVE ↓CLASSIFY ↓DIAGNOSE ↓PATCH ↓RUN AGAIN
Preserve the original failure evidence.
Do not overwrite the evidence with only the final successful state.
==================================================NINETY-FIFTH: WORKER FAILURE
If a worker fails:
do not immediately spawn unlimited replacements.
Determine:
failure typeremaining budgetwhether the task is still validwhether another worker is appropriatewhether the main session should take over
Terminate failed workers cleanly.
Preserve useful evidence.
==================================================NINETY-SIXTH: PARALLELIZATION THRESHOLD
Parallelize only when:
tasks are genuinely independent+the coordination cost is justified.
Good candidate:
three independent repository investigations.
Poor candidate:
three workers editing the same function.
Poor candidate:
tiny five-minute task.
The goal is increased throughput, not maximum worker count.
==================================================NINETY-SEVENTH: SYNTHESIS AFTER PARALLEL WORK
Parallel worker results must return to a central synthesis point.
The synthesis process:
collect→ normalize→ compare→ detect conflicts→ inspect evidence→ select/synthesize→ implement intentionally
Do not blindly concatenate worker outputs.
==================================================NINETY-EIGHTH: RESEARCH QUALITY
When external research is required:
prefer authoritative sources.
Separate:
FACTINFERENCEHYPOTHESISRECOMMENDATION
Do not turn an unverified claim into architecture.
For technical libraries:
prefer official documentation and current version information.
Use Context7 where appropriate.
==================================================NINETY-NINTH: MECHANISM EXTRACTION
When studying an external project:
do not ask only:
"What does this project do?"
Ask:
"What mechanism makes this useful?"
Extract:
mechanismproblem solvedinputsoutputsstatealgorithmtradeoffslimitationsresource requirementsfailure modesintegration pattern
Then determine:
Can Jarvis use it directly?
Should Jarvis adapt it?
Should Jarvis redesign it?
Should Jarvis reject it?
==================================================ONE-HUNDREDTH: JARVIS-NATIVE REDESIGN
External mechanisms should pass through:
EXTERNAL TOOL ↓RESEARCH ↓MECHANISM EXTRACTION ↓ADVANTAGES ↓LIMITATIONS ↓JARVIS REQUIREMENTS ↓NATIVE DESIGN ↓IMPLEMENTATION
Do not simply install a framework and call that Jarvis evolution.
Jarvis should absorb useful mechanisms into its own architecture when justified.

→ resolve executables

Exactly — there is a simpler way, but the distinction is that Claude Code's "auto/manual" permission behavior is controlled by its permission mode, not by a normal auto command-line flag.
When Claude Code starts, it can operate in modes such as:

Default/manual → asks you before potentially dangerous actions.
Accept edits → automatically accepts file edits but can still ask for other permissions.
Plan → analyzes/plans without making changes.
Don't ask / bypass permissions → automatically proceeds.

The reason I pointed you toward:
claude --dangerously-skip-permissions

is because that's the non-interactive bypass mode. But Claude Code intentionally refuses that mode when running as root.
So your observation is correct: the Claude Code interface can present a permission-mode choice, but the fully automatic mode is deliberately protected when you're root.
And importantly, you don't need to rebuild your entire Jarvis environment just to get this behavior.
If your goal is simply:

The 3D World isn't the algorithm
Zoey's 3D workspace is useful for presence and observability, but I wouldn't treat it as a cognitive innovation. It visualizes tasks, companions and activity in real time. 
For Jarvis:

   ↓
visualize nervous-system state
   ↓
show attention

That's much more aligned with your existing Orb concept.
And one interesting integration mechanism
Zoey lets Architect users connect custom REST APIs or MCP servers, so its companion layer can act through external systems. 
Jarvis already wants essentially the same idea, but with a stronger architecture:
Capability
   ↓
Adapter
   ↓
REST / MCP / local API / process / device

So again, mechanism → Jarvis-native redesign, not copying Zoey.
What I would actually add to Jarvis
I would take five mechanisms from Zoey:
1. Hierarchical delegation
   Jarvis → specialist → bounded worker

2. Skill-context coupling
   skill + memory + current state → execution

3. Adaptive specialist routing
   intent → best capability/specialist

4. Reusable automation pipeline
   trigger → same cognitive/capability machinery

5. Live operational visibility
   nervous system → Orb/presence → visible activity

Zoey companions as permanent personalities
200 fixed agents
Zoey's proprietary memory architecture
Zoey's 3D world as the core architecture
Zoey's platform-specific orchestration

Because Jarvis already has stronger concepts for these areas.
Bottom line
Yes, Zoey has useful algorithms/mechanisms for Jarvis — especially hierarchical delegation, contextual skill execution, adaptive specialist routing, reusable automation, and activity observability.
The most interesting one is:

Intent → specialist → bounded workers → aggregation → synthesis

That could improve your existing Capability Fabric + PlanGraph + Worker Orchestration + Nervous System without adding another agent framework. Zoey's docs directly support the delegation/specialization/parallel-execution model. 
I would classify Zoey in your research vault as “mechanism source — orchestration/skill/context/automation,” not as a dependency.

That is much closer to the living memory you're trying to build than “put messages in a vector DB.”
Current work supports exactly this direction: Hindsight combines fact/experience/observation/opinion networks with temporal graphs and hybrid retrieval; Graphiti combines semantic, keyword and graph retrieval with temporal provenance; LangMem explicitly supports both foreground/hot-path and background memory management; and recent memory research is moving toward structured, temporal and self-editable memory rather than flat chat-history retrieval. 
What I would actually mark for Jarvis
I would divide this huge atlas into:
A — Implement soon
Memory candidate scoring, atomic memory, semantic/episodic/procedural classification, hybrid retrieval, temporal retrieval, graph traversal, importance/recency/utility ranking, contradiction detection, deduplication, memory consolidation, context budgeting, failure memory, decision memory.
B — Research + experiment
Hindsight-style networks, Graphiti-style temporal graph, GraphRAG/Leiden, associative retrieval, MMR/RRF, HyDE, tree/hierarchical memory, FSRS-derived retention, bandit-based capability routing, adaptive model routing.
C — Later evolution
Bayesian optimization, evolutionary algorithm discovery, MAP-Elites, genetic programming, program synthesis, automated repair, causal discovery, self-architecture search.
D — Stage 16 / diagnostics
Isolation Forest, CUSUM, EWMA, change-point detection, dependency-fault propagation, anomaly clustering, automated root-cause analysis.

and then let the Building System select which candidate algorithms to actually implement and benchmark.
That gives you what you originally wanted: Jarvis doesn't inherit one memory algorithm or one routing algorithm; he gains an algorithmic toolbox and the ability to discover which mechanism is best for each organ.

Yes. Since we're switching away from Claude Code + OmniRoute, I would set up Cline as the new development engine, but do it cleanly and without dragging the old stack along.
I checked the current Cline CLI docs/repository. The current CLI is 3.x, runs natively on Linux ARM64, supports interactive and headless operation, has --yolo for skipping tool approvals, native MCP, sub-agents/teams, checkpoints, scheduled runs, and can use Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini/OpenRouter/Ollama/OpenAI-compatible providers.

STEP 3 — Configure the model
You have three sensible choices.

Don't put your real key into a prompt you send me.
Option B — OpenRouter
Cline supports OpenRouter directly. 
This is useful if you want model choice without OmniRoute.
Option C — Local Ollama

The most important architectural principle
The uploaded material, the algorithm research, and the previous Jarvis architecture all converge on one idea:
Do not make intelligence equal to the model.
Make intelligence the organized system of memory + algorithms + models + capabilities + state + experience + self-evaluation + adaptation.
Then Jarvis can eventually replace any individual part without ceasing to be Jarvis.
And the external Cline/LFM setup you're doing now is only scaffolding to reach that point. The endgame is that Jarvis's own Builder becomes the thing that discovers, builds, tests, repairs, replaces, and eventually redesigns the system.

ChatGPT:
You're right about the goal, but there is an important distinction:
You don't want to make the 1.2B model magically “become LFM.” LFM is already a model architecture. What you actually want is to build a Jarvis-specific small model/brain that inherits useful behavior from stronger models while retaining a low resource footprint.
And the Aider failure is a separate issue: your pip is trying to build uv for Android's Python 3.14 ABI, and that installation path isn't working in this Ubuntu/Termux setup. So drop Aider too. We don't need to solve that tonight.
The truth about turning your models into a better LFM-like brain
There are three different things people often mix together:
1. Quantization
7B model
→ Q4
→ much smaller RAM
→ same underlying model, lower numerical precision

That's not turning it into an LFM.
2. Distillation
STRONG TEACHER
      ↓
student training
      ↓
SMALL MODEL

This is much closer to what you're describing.
Liquid AI itself says its LFM2 training used a larger LFM1-7B teacher and knowledge distillation as part of training the smaller model. 
So the idea is real.
3. Architecture redesign
This is the part that is actually your Jarvis idea.
You don't just compress a model. You identify:
reasoning
tool use
memory
planning
retrieval
routing
compression

and decide which parts should be:
small neural model
+
deterministic algorithms
+
retrieval
+
specialized model
+
cached knowledge

That can produce a much smaller computational system without requiring one giant model to do everything.
That's where I think Jarvis becomes interesting.

What I would build
Not:
Qwen3 1.7B
→ "convert to LFM"

Instead:
Teacher intelligence
      ↓
Behavior / skill extraction
      ↓
Training dataset
      ↓
Distillation
      ↓
Small student model
      ↓
Deterministic mechanisms around it
      ↓
Jarvis-native compact brain

The compact brain
                JARVIS COMPACT BRAIN
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        │              │              │
      SMALL LLM     RETRIEVAL      ALGORITHMS
        │              │              │
        └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                       │
                MEMORY / STATE
                       │
                  TOOL ROUTER
                       │
                  BRAIN OUTPUT

The model doesn't need to remember everything.
It doesn't need to calculate everything.
It doesn't need to route everything.
That is how you reduce resource pressure without reducing the entire system to a weak model.

And you already have the right raw material
You currently have:
LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
Qwen3-1.7B-Q4_K_M.gguf

Liquid AI's published results show the 1.2B LFM2.5 is unusually strong for its size and specifically optimized for on-device use; they report 719 MB memory for Q4_0 on a Snapdragon Gen4 CPU benchmark. 
They also publish a LFM2.5-1.2B-Thinking model under 900 MB for on-device reasoning. 
So LFM2.5 is a much better starting point for your phone than trying to force a generic 7B-class model into the role of an always-resident brain.

But don't train anything on the phone
This is the key decision I'd make.
Your phone should be the:
inference / execution device
not the:

Training/distillation should happen somewhere with substantially more compute.
The phone can then receive:
student model
+
adapters
+
retrieval index
+
skills

Jarvis state

and run it locally.

Instead of:
1.2B → 7B → 14B → 32B

you want:
1.2B model

better training

specialized adapters

retrieval

#!/bin/bash

set -e

LLAMA="/root/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server"
MODEL_DIR="/sdcard/jarvis-repo/vault/just_downloaded"

stop_models() {
    pkill -x llama-server 2>/dev/null || true
    sleep 2
}

start_lfm() {
    stop_models
    exec "$LLAMA" \
      -m "$MODEL_DIR/LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf" \
      --host 127.0.0.1 \
      --port 8080 \
      -c 4096 \
      -ngl 0 \
      -np 1
}

start_qwen() {
    stop_models
    exec "$LLAMA" \
      -m "$MODEL_DIR/Qwen3-1.7B-Q4_K_M.gguf" \
      --host 127.0.0.1 \
      --port 8080 \
      -c 4096 \
      -ngl 0 \
      -np 1
}

case "${1:-}" in
    lfm)
        start_lfm
        ;;
    qwen)
        start_qwen
        ;;
    stop)
        stop_models
        ;;
    *)
        echo "Usage: $0 {lfm|qwen|stop}"
        exit 1
        ;;
esac
EOF

chmod +x scripts/jarvis-model.sh

set -e

LLAMA="/root/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server"
MODEL_DIR="/sdcard/jarvis-repo/vault/just_downloaded"

LFM="$MODEL_DIR/LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf"
QWEN="$MODEL_DIR/Qwen3-1.7B-Q4_K_M.gguf"

stop_model() {
    pkill -x llama-server 2>/dev/null || true
    sleep 2
}

health() {

}

      -m "$LFM" \

      --port 8080 \
      -c 4096 \
      -ngl 0 \
      -np 1
}

    stop_model

    "$LLAMA" \
      -m "$QWEN" \
      --host 127.0.0.1 \
      --port 8080 \
      -c 4096 \
      -ngl 0 \

  qwen)
    start_qwen
    ;;
  stop)
    stop_model
    ;;
  health)
    if health; then
      echo "MODEL SERVER: ONLINE"
    else
      echo "MODEL SERVER: OFFLINE"
      exit 1
    fi
    ;;
  *)
    echo "Usage: bash $0 {lfm|qwen|stop|health}"
    exit 1
    ;;
esac

import json
import urllib.request
import urllib.error

MODEL_SERVER = "http://127.0.0.1:8080"

def chat(messages, max_tokens=256, temperature=0.2):
    payload = {
        "model": "jarvis-local",
        "messages": messages,
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        "temperature": temperature
    }

    request = urllib.request.Request(
        MODEL_SERVER + "/v1/chat/completions",
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        method="POST"
    )

    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=120) as response:
            data = json.loads(response.read().decode())

        return data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

    except Exception as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Local model gateway failed: {e}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = chat([
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Reply exactly: JARVIS MODEL GATEWAY ONLINE"
        }
    ])

    print(result)

One correction to our architecture
We shouldn't make LFM permanently resident just because it's the smallest model.
Your measured result was ~783 MiB RSS, while your phone had only ~2.3 GiB available with substantial swap activity. That's workable, but Jarvis's runtime, Android, memory, voice models, browser automation, databases, etc. will also need resources.
So the eventual policy should be:
                 JARVIS MODEL GATEWAY
                         │
                         ▼
                 RESOURCE GOVERNOR
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              │                     │
          LFM loaded            Qwen loaded
          when useful           when useful
              │                     │
              └──────────┬──────────┘
                         │
                    unload/reload
                    according to
                    task + RAM +
                    thermal + battery

Not: "LFM always stays loaded."
That's a critical distinction for the Jarvis architecture you're trying to build.

cat > runtime/model_gateway/model_controller.py <<'PY'
import json
import os
import signal
import subprocess
import time
import urllib.request
import urllib.error

REPO = "/sdcard/jarvis-repo"
LLAMA = "/root/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server"
MODEL_DIR = f"{REPO}/vault/just_downloaded"

MODELS = {
    "lfm": {
        "id": "lfm2.5-1.2b-instruct",
        "path": f"{MODEL_DIR}/LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf",
        "port": 8080,
    },
    "qwen": {
        "id": "qwen3-1.7b",
        "path": f"{MODEL_DIR}/Qwen3-1.7B-Q4_K_M.gguf",
        "port": 8080,
    },
}


def server_running():
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(
            "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health",
            timeout=2
        ) as r:
            return r.status == 200
    except Exception:
        return False


def current_processes():
    try:
        result = subprocess.check_output(
            ["pgrep", "-af", "llama-server"],
            text=True
        )
        return result.strip()
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError:
        return ""


def stop():
    subprocess.run(
        ["pkill", "-x", "llama-server"],
        stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
        stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL,
    )

    for _ in range(20):
        if not current_processes():
            return True
        time.sleep(0.25)

    return False


def start(name):
    if name not in MODELS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown model: {name}")

    model = MODELS[name]

    stop()

    command = [
        LLAMA,
        "-m", model["path"],
        "--host", "127.0.0.1",
        "--port", str(model["port"]),
        "-c", "4096",
        "-ngl", "0",
        "-np", "1",
    ]

    process = subprocess.Popen(
        command,
        stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL,
        stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL,
        start_new_session=True,
    )

    for _ in range(120):
        if server_running():
            return {
                "status": "online",
                "model": name,
                "pid": process.pid,
                "port": model["port"],
            }

        if process.poll() is not None:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Model process exited with code {process.returncode}"
            )

        time.sleep(0.5)

    process.kill()
    raise RuntimeError("Timed out waiting for model server")


def status():
    return {
        "server_online": server_running(),
        "processes": current_processes(),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(status(), indent=2))

Step 3 — Make the gateway identify the active model
Your current gateway blindly sends:
"model": "jarvis-local"

That's acceptable for now, but the gateway should know which local model is actually active.
Replace it with:
cat > runtime/model_gateway/gateway.py <<'PY'
import json
import urllib.request
import urllib.error

MODEL_SERVER = "http://127.0.0.1:8080"


def health():
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(
            MODEL_SERVER + "/health",
            timeout=3
        ) as response:
            return response.status == 200
    except Exception:
        return False


def active_model():
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        MODEL_SERVER + "/v1/models",
        method="GET"
    )

    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=5) as response:
        data = json.loads(response.read().decode())

    models = data.get("data", [])

    if not models:
        return None

    return models[0].get("id")


def chat(messages, max_tokens=256, temperature=0.2):
    if not health():
        raise RuntimeError("Local model server is offline")

    payload = {
        "model": "jarvis-local",
        "messages": messages,
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        "temperature": temperature
    }

    request = urllib.request.Request(
        MODEL_SERVER + "/v1/chat/completions",
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        method="POST"
    )

    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=120) as response:
            data = json.loads(response.read().decode())

        return data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

    except Exception as e:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"Local model gateway failed: {e}"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("HEALTH:", health())
    print("MODEL:", active_model())

    result = chat([
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are the local cognitive substrate of JARVIS. "
                "Follow instructions precisely."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Reply exactly: JARVIS SUBSTRATE ONLINE"
        }
    ], max_tokens=20, temperature=0)

    print("RESPONSE:", repr(result))

~1.0 GiB RSS

while Android + Termux + Ubuntu + everything else is already consuming substantial memory.
So the correct architecture is:
Resident
LFM
Fast response / routing / lightweight reasoning / fallback.
On demand
Qwen
Load only when the task requires capabilities that justify its additional RAM and latency.
Then unload it.

Task
 ↓
Task classifier

Can LFM handle it?

 └── NO
       ↓
   Load Qwen
       ↓
   Execute task
       ↓
   Verify result
       ↓
   Unload Qwen
       ↓
   Return to LFM

That is the beginning of your model lifecycle system.

#!/bin/bash
set -e

REPO="/sdcard/jarvis-repo"
LLAMA="/root/llama.cpp/build/bin/llama-server"
MODEL="$REPO/vault/just_downloaded/LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf"
PORT=8080

echo "=== JARVIS LOCAL STARTUP ==="
echo "Repository: $REPO"
echo "Model: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct-Q4_K_M"
echo "Endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:$PORT"

if pgrep -x llama-server >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "llama-server already running."
else
    echo "Starting LFM..."
    "$LLAMA" \
      -m "$MODEL" \
      --host 127.0.0.1 \
      --port "$PORT" \
      -c 4096 \
      -ngl 0 \
      -np 1 \
      > "$REPO/logs_lfm_server.txt" 2>&1 &
fi

echo "Waiting for model server..."

for i in $(seq 1 120); do
    if curl -sf "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/health" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo "JARVIS LOCAL MODEL: ONLINE"
        exit 0
    fi
    sleep 0.5
done

echo "ERROR: model server did not become ready."
echo "Check: $REPO/logs_lfm_server.txt"
exit 1
EOF
